newsitem.title: USA: Members of Congress back Iraq air strikes.
newsitem.headline: Members of Congress back Iraq air strikes.

text.p: Members of Congress on Tuesday backed U.S. cruise missile strikes against Iraq, saying President Saddam Hussein had to be taught a lesson.
President Bill Clinton ordered the air strikes after Saddam reportedly ignored demands to cease an attack against Kurds in northern Iraq and withdraw his troops.

He acted as members of Congress drifted back to Washington to begin what was expected to be a highly political runup to the Nov. 5 elections, although politics is usually suspended at the water's edge when American troops are in action.
Nevertheless, some Republicans took a swipe at Clinton's policies, while applauding the military action.

New York Republican Rep. Benjamin Gilman, chairman of the House International Relations Committee, said the strikes were a "regrettable necessity" caused by the administration's "diplomatic deafness" in failing to give high-level attention to developments in Iraq.
And Sen. Richard Lugar, an Indiana Republican and a senior member of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee, said Clinton had to go further in acting militarily against Saddam.

Republican House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich praised the "exemplary professionalism" of the U.S. military and said he hoped Saddam "has learned that his brazen defiance of the international community and his brutal treament of the Kurdish minority in Iran will not go unpunished."
Gingrich added in a statement: "Now that we have acted, we need to be resolute and consistent in the application of that lesson."

Republican Sen. John McCain of Arizona, a key ally of Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole and a frequent critic of Clinton's foreign policies, supported the troops and added in a statement: "Any further discussion of the policies that resulted in this action should await its conclusion."
The Senate may vote on Wednesday on a resolution expected to support the U.S. military action and criticize Saddam.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said he hoped for broad bipartisan support for such a resolution and an aide to Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said Lott was working with Daschle on it.

Daschle said the United States had reduced Saddam's threat to others and had shown its allies it would protect its interests. "I hope that Saddam Hussein and those who are in control in the Iraqi government clearly understand the resolution of this administration and this country," he said.
Lugar criticized "inadequate" U.S. diplomacy and called for a "well-planned, disproportionate and devastating response" that would leave Saddam's regime "mortally wounded."

But Republican Sen. Phil Gramm of Texas, while supporting Clinton's action, warned against the United States being drawn into any conflict between Iran and Iraq sparked by their support of warring Kurdish factions.
"We do not have a dog in that fight," Gramm said.
